newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fire-hit Channel Tunnel reopens for passenger cars.
newsitem.headline: Fire-hit Channel Tunnel reopens for passenger cars.

text.p: Passenger car shuttle services resumed through the Anglo-French Channel tunnel on Tuesday, three weeks after a fire closed the undersea rail link.
French investigators denied reports in the British press that arson caused the accident on November 18 which forced the closing of the 50-km (30-mile) tunnel to all traffic.
Fire on a truck destroyed a freight vehicle shuttle train and severely damaged a section of the tunnel. Thirty-four people were injured.

The first Le Shuttle train to go through the tunnel since the fire, carrying 61 vehicles, left the Coquelles terminal near Calais at 7:30 a.m. (0630 GMT) and arrived at the Cheriton terminal in southeastern England 50 minutes later, about 15 minutes longer than was required before the accident because of damage in the twin-bore tunnel.
Rail services for passengers between Paris and London and Brussels and London resumed last Wednesday. No date has been set for a resumption of the shuttle service for trucks.

The judge in charge of an investigation of the fire and other sources denied a report in Tuesday's Evening Standard headlined "It Was Arson" and saying a preliminary report was expected to conclude that the fire was set on purpose.

The newspaper said a major development was expected "within days." But a source close to the investigators said it was impossible to say what had caused the fire and it would probably not be known for weeks.

"Nothing so far enables us to determine the cause or the circumstances of the fire," the source, who asked not to be named, told Reuters. "The experts...have not yet drawn any conclusions and we will have to wait several weeks (before they do)," he added.

Passengers boarding Tuesday's first car train brushed aside safety concerns after the fire and a bomb on a Paris city train by suspected Algerian Moslem militants last week that killed four people and injured more than 90.

"I don't see why we should be frightened," said Bruno, a trader in charcoal who lives in Lille in northern France and works in London. "When a plane crashes or when two trains collide, it doesn't stop other planes or trains from leaving.
"The Shuttle is faster than other means of transport across the Channel and it's more reliable in terms of timetables," he added.
The crossings for car passengers using Le Shuttle will be from five to 15 minutes longer than normal.
And until December 19, only half as many trains will run as before the accident with one leaving in each direction every 40 minutes, a Eurotunnel spokesman said.
The reopening of the passenger car service was welcomed by shopkeepers near the tunnel terminal in Calais, northern France, who rely heavily on people using the trains.
The turnover of a shopping district located near the Calais terminal has dropped by some 30 per cent in the last three weeks.
The initial train slowed down twice during Tuesday's crossing to move from one of the parallel rail tunnels to the other one, to avoid the damaged section, which is still undergoing repairs.
